title: Physical Chemistry II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L physical chemistry curriculum, second semester: electrochemistry (cells, electrode potentials, Nernst equation, conductance), solutions and colligative properties, phase equilibria, and surface chemistry/catalysis. Builds on CHM201's thermodynamics/kinetics/gas-law/equilibrium foundation without repeating that material.

questions.question: In an electrochemical (galvanic) cell, at which electrode does oxidation occur?
options: The anode
The cathode
Both electrodes equally
Neither electrode
questions.correct_answer: The anode
questions.explanation: By convention, oxidation (loss of electrons) always occurs at the anode, while reduction occurs at the cathode, in both galvanic and electrolytic cells.

questions.question: What is the function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell such as the Daniell cell?
options: To maintain electrical neutrality by allowing ion flow between the two half-cells
To supply electrons directly to the external circuit
To increase the voltage produced by the cell
To prevent any current from flowing
questions.correct_answer: To maintain electrical neutrality by allowing ion flow between the two half-cells
questions.explanation: As the cell reaction proceeds, charge would build up in each half-cell without the salt bridge; it allows spectator ions to migrate and maintain electrical neutrality, keeping the cell functioning.

questions.question: The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is assigned a standard reduction potential of what value, by convention?
questions.explanation: The standard hydrogen electrode is defined as the reference point with E° = 0.00 V, against which all other standard electrode potentials are measured.

questions.question: For a cell with E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode, if E°cathode = +0.34 V (Cu2+/Cu) and E°anode = -0.76 V (Zn2+/Zn), what is E°cell?
questions.explanation: E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V, matching the well-known standard potential of the Daniell cell.

questions.question: What does the Nernst equation allow chemists to calculate?
options: The cell potential under non-standard conditions of concentration and temperature
The rate of an electrochemical reaction
The equilibrium constant of a gas-phase reaction only
The pH of a buffer solution
questions.correct_answer: The cell potential under non-standard conditions of concentration and temperature
questions.explanation: The Nernst equation, E = E° - (RT/nF)lnQ, relates the actual cell potential to the standard potential, temperature, and the reaction quotient, allowing calculation under non-standard conditions.

questions.question: In the Nernst equation, what happens to the cell potential as the reaction quotient Q increases (i.e., as products accumulate)?
options: The cell potential decreases
The cell potential increases
The cell potential remains constant
The cell potential becomes infinite
questions.correct_answer: The cell potential decreases
questions.explanation: As Q increases toward the equilibrium constant K, the logarithmic term in the Nernst equation grows, reducing E; at equilibrium, Q = K and E = 0.

questions.question: Which law of electrolysis states that the mass of a substance liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electric charge passed?
options: Faraday's first law of electrolysis
Faraday's second law of electrolysis
Ohm's law
Raoult's law
questions.correct_answer: Faraday's first law of electrolysis
questions.explanation: Faraday's first law states that mass deposited or liberated (m) is proportional to the quantity of charge (Q) passed through the electrolyte, expressed as m = ZQ, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent.

questions.question: What is molar conductivity, and how does it typically change as the concentration of a weak electrolyte solution decreases?
options: Conductivity per mole of electrolyte; it increases with dilution due to greater degree of dissociation
Conductivity per mole of electrolyte; it decreases with dilution
Conductivity per litre of solvent only; unaffected by dilution
Conductivity measured only at infinite concentration
questions.correct_answer: Conductivity per mole of electrolyte; it increases with dilution due to greater degree of dissociation
questions.explanation: For weak electrolytes, dilution increases the degree of dissociation, releasing more ions per mole and thus increasing molar conductivity as concentration decreases.

questions.question: Which colligative property is defined as the lowering of the vapour pressure of a solvent caused by the addition of a non-volatile solute?
options: Relative lowering of vapour pressure
Boiling point elevation
Freezing point depression
Osmotic pressure
questions.correct_answer: Relative lowering of vapour pressure
questions.explanation: The relative lowering of vapour pressure is a colligative property describing how a non-volatile solute reduces the vapour pressure of the solvent, as described quantitatively by Raoult's law.

questions.question: Raoult's law relates the partial vapour pressure of a component in an ideal solution to which quantity?
options: Its mole fraction in the solution multiplied by its pure vapour pressure
Its mass fraction in the solution only
The total pressure of the system
The temperature of the solution only
questions.correct_answer: Its mole fraction in the solution multiplied by its pure vapour pressure
questions.explanation: Raoult's law states that the partial vapour pressure of a solvent equals its mole fraction multiplied by the vapour pressure of the pure solvent, for an ideal solution.

questions.question: Why does dissolving a non-volatile solute in a solvent raise the boiling point of the resulting solution compared to the pure solvent?
options: The solute lowers the vapour pressure, so a higher temperature is needed to reach atmospheric pressure and boil
The solute increases the vapour pressure of the solvent
The solute reacts chemically with the solvent to form a new compound with higher boiling point
Boiling point elevation only occurs with volatile solutes
questions.correct_answer: The solute lowers the vapour pressure, so a higher temperature is needed to reach atmospheric pressure and boil
questions.explanation: Since the non-volatile solute reduces the solvent's vapour pressure at any given temperature, a higher temperature is required for the vapour pressure to equal atmospheric pressure, elevating the boiling point.

questions.question: What is osmotic pressure?
options: The minimum pressure needed to prevent the net flow of solvent across a semipermeable membrane into a solution
The pressure exerted by a gas trapped in a solution
The vapour pressure of a pure solvent
The pressure at which a solid melts
questions.correct_answer: The minimum pressure needed to prevent the net flow of solvent across a semipermeable membrane into a solution
questions.explanation: Osmotic pressure is the external pressure that must be applied to a solution to just stop osmosis, the net movement of solvent molecules through a semipermeable membrane from a region of lower to higher solute concentration.

questions.question: The van't Hoff factor (i) is used to correct colligative property equations for which type of solute?
options: Electrolytes that dissociate into multiple ions in solution
Non-electrolytes that do not dissociate at all
Solutes that are completely insoluble
Gaseous solutes only
questions.correct_answer: Electrolytes that dissociate into multiple ions in solution
questions.explanation: The van't Hoff factor accounts for the number of particles an electrolyte produces upon dissociation (e.g., i = 2 for NaCl), since colligative properties depend on the total number of solute particles.

questions.question: A phase diagram of a pure substance typically shows the boundaries between solid, liquid, and gas phases. What does the triple point on a phase diagram represent?
options: The unique temperature and pressure at which all three phases coexist in equilibrium
The temperature at which the substance decomposes
The pressure at which the substance becomes an ideal gas
The point at which the substance has zero entropy
questions.correct_answer: The unique temperature and pressure at which all three phases coexist in equilibrium
questions.explanation: The triple point is a specific, unique combination of temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid, and gas phases of a pure substance exist simultaneously in equilibrium.

questions.question: What is the critical point on a phase diagram?
options: The temperature and pressure beyond which distinct liquid and gas phases no longer exist
The point where a substance is completely solid
The point at which a substance has its lowest possible temperature
The point where two solids are in equilibrium
questions.correct_answer: The temperature and pressure beyond which distinct liquid and gas phases no longer exist
questions.explanation: Above the critical temperature and pressure, the distinction between liquid and gas disappears, and the substance exists as a supercritical fluid.

questions.question: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation relates vapour pressure to which other variable, allowing prediction of how vapour pressure changes with conditions?
options: Temperature
Molar mass
Density
Refractive index
questions.correct_answer: Temperature
questions.explanation: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation describes how the vapour pressure of a substance varies with absolute temperature, incorporating the enthalpy of vaporization.

questions.question: According to the phase rule, F = C - P + 2, for a single-component system (C=1) existing as two phases in equilibrium (P=2), how many degrees of freedom (F) does the system have?
questions.explanation: F = C - P + 2 = 1 - 2 + 2 = 1, meaning only one intensive variable (e.g., temperature) can be varied independently while the two phases remain in equilibrium; pressure is then fixed.

questions.question: What is the general term for a substance that lowers the surface tension of a liquid when dissolved in it, such as soap in water?
options: Surfactant
Catalyst
Electrolyte
Buffer
questions.correct_answer: Surfactant
questions.explanation: A surfactant (surface-active agent) reduces the surface tension between two phases by adsorbing at the interface, as soap molecules do at the air-water interface.

questions.question: In heterogeneous catalysis, such as the Haber process using an iron catalyst, where does the catalytic reaction primarily take place?
options: On the surface of the solid catalyst, where gas molecules are adsorbed
Throughout the entire volume of the catalyst uniformly
In the gas phase only, away from the catalyst surface
Inside the crystal lattice of the catalyst
questions.correct_answer: On the surface of the solid catalyst, where gas molecules are adsorbed
questions.explanation: Heterogeneous catalysis occurs at the catalyst surface, where reactant gas molecules are adsorbed, weakening their bonds and lowering the activation energy for reaction before products desorb.

questions.question: What distinguishes physical adsorption (physisorption) from chemical adsorption (chemisorption) on a solid surface?
options: Physisorption involves weak van der Waals forces, while chemisorption involves the formation of chemical bonds
Physisorption always requires higher temperatures than chemisorption
Chemisorption is always reversible while physisorption is not
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.correct_answer: Physisorption involves weak van der Waals forces, while chemisorption involves the formation of chemical bonds
questions.explanation: Physisorption is a weak, reversible interaction due to van der Waals forces with low enthalpy of adsorption, while chemisorption involves stronger, often irreversible chemical bond formation with much higher enthalpy of adsorption.

questions.question: Which type of colloid is formed when a liquid is dispersed in a gas, such as fog or mist?
options: Aerosol
Emulsion
Sol
Gel
questions.correct_answer: Aerosol
questions.explanation: An aerosol is a colloidal dispersion of liquid or solid particles in a gas; fog is specifically a liquid-in-gas aerosol.

questions.question: The Tyndall effect, the scattering of light by colloidal particles, is used to distinguish a colloid from what other type of mixture?
options: A true solution
Another colloid
A pure element
A pure compound
questions.correct_answer: A true solution
questions.explanation: Colloidal particles are large enough to scatter light (Tyndall effect), while true solutions have particles too small to scatter light, so a visible light beam passes through a true solution without scattering.

questions.question: For a weak electrolyte such as acetic acid, how does molar conductivity at infinite dilution relate to Kohlrausch's law?
options: It can be calculated by summing the individual ionic conductivities at infinite dilution
It is always equal to zero
It cannot be determined for weak electrolytes at all
It equals the molar conductivity at any concentration
questions.correct_answer: It can be calculated by summing the individual ionic conductivities at infinite dilution
questions.explanation: Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions allows the molar conductivity at infinite dilution for a weak electrolyte to be calculated by combining the limiting ionic conductivities of its constituent ions, even though it cannot be measured directly by extrapolation for weak electrolytes.

questions.question: What happens to the freezing point of a solvent when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in it, compared to the pure solvent?
options: The freezing point is depressed (lowered)
The freezing point is elevated (raised)
The freezing point remains exactly the same
The freezing point becomes impossible to measure
questions.correct_answer: The freezing point is depressed (lowered)
questions.explanation: Dissolving a solute disrupts the regular arrangement needed for the solvent to freeze, so a lower temperature is required to establish equilibrium between solid and liquid phases, depressing the freezing point.

questions.question: Which electrode reaction correctly represents reduction at the cathode of a standard Daniell cell (Zn/Zn2+ || Cu2+/Cu)?
options: Cu2+(aq) + 2e- -> Cu(s)
Zn(s) -> Zn2+(aq) + 2e-
Cu(s) -> Cu2+(aq) + 2e-
Zn2+(aq) + 2e- -> Zn(s)
questions.correct_answer: Cu2+(aq) + 2e- -> Cu(s)
questions.explanation: In the Daniell cell, copper is the cathode where reduction of Cu2+ ions to solid copper occurs, while zinc is the anode where oxidation takes place.

questions.question: What term describes a solution that obeys Raoult's law across the entire range of concentration?
options: An ideal solution
A saturated solution
A supersaturated solution
A colloidal solution
questions.correct_answer: An ideal solution
questions.explanation: An ideal solution is one in which the interactions between different molecules are essentially the same as between like molecules, so the solution obeys Raoult's law over the whole concentration range.

questions.question: A solution of glucose is separated from pure water by a semipermeable membrane. In which direction does osmosis cause net water movement?
options: From the pure water into the glucose solution
From the glucose solution into the pure water
There is no net movement since glucose is a non-electrolyte
Water moves equally in both directions with no net flow
questions.correct_answer: From the pure water into the glucose solution
questions.explanation: Osmosis drives solvent (water) to move from a region of lower solute concentration (pure water) to higher solute concentration (glucose solution) across the semipermeable membrane, diluting the solution.

questions.question: In electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, what product forms at the cathode?
options: Sodium metal, by reduction of Na+ ions
Chlorine gas, by oxidation of Cl- ions
Oxygen gas
Hydrogen gas
questions.correct_answer: Sodium metal, by reduction of Na+ ions
questions.explanation: During electrolysis of molten NaCl, Na+ ions migrate to the cathode and are reduced to sodium metal, while Cl- ions migrate to the anode and are oxidized to chlorine gas.

questions.question: What is the significance of the electrochemical series, a ranking of standard electrode potentials?
options: It allows prediction of the relative oxidizing and reducing strengths of different species and the feasibility of redox reactions
It ranks elements only by atomic mass
It shows only the melting points of metals
It has no practical predictive use in chemistry
questions.correct_answer: It allows prediction of the relative oxidizing and reducing strengths of different species and the feasibility of redox reactions
questions.explanation: The electrochemical series orders half-reactions by standard reduction potential, allowing chemists to predict which species will act as oxidizing or reducing agents and whether a redox reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

questions.question: Why do catalysts not appear in the overall balanced equation of a reaction despite taking part in the reaction mechanism?
options: A catalyst is regenerated unchanged at the end of the reaction, so it cancels out of the overall equation
Catalysts do not actually participate in the reaction mechanism at all
Catalysts are always gases and are ignored in equations
Catalysts change into completely different substances that are not written
questions.correct_answer: A catalyst is regenerated unchanged at the end of the reaction, so it cancels out of the overall equation
questions.explanation: Although a catalyst actively participates in intermediate steps of the mechanism, it is fully regenerated by the end of the reaction, so it does not appear as a net reactant or product in the overall equation.
